newsitem.title: CHINA: China moves to manage money supply by market means.
newsitem.headline: China moves to manage money supply by market means.

text.p: China is making basic changes to the control of money supply, allowing greater play to market forces to make the system more responsive to fast-changing conditions in the Chinese economy, bankers said on Thursday.

They said changes so far included allowing state banks more control over asset-liabilty management, in effect giving them the power to refuse working capital loans to customers if their account balance does not justify it.
Up to the end of last year, state-owned enterprises were allowed to borrow as much as they liked from the major state banks, within overall limits set by the central state planners.

Beijing officials have also said they plan a major expansion this year of the local currency interbank market and of open market operations to provide more sophisticated means of controlling the amounts of cash flowing through the economy.
"The main problem with the old system (of money supply control) is that the statistics always lag behind real economic development," said a banker in Beijing with the Agricultural Bank of China.
But the inefficiencies of the centrally-planned economy are gradually being eased by transferring more responsibilities to the state banks, bankers said.

"All major state banks have started to manage their current accounts on an asset-debt ratio basis as an experiment," a Beijing-based banker with the Construction Bank of China said. "We expect the arrangement to be formalised in 1998."
"Through this experiment, the central bank is moving to allow us state banks to be more independent in management terms," said the banker with the Agricultural Bank.
"This is one of a number of steps being taken by the central bank to use market means to control money supply," he added.
Beijing manages money supply by setting quotas for loans by major state banks. It has yet to abolish the loan quota system on fixed asset investment, bankers said.

"The system still contains elements left over from the planned economy, in which the key task for our major state banks was to fulfill the state's macro-economic targets," said a banker with the Bank of China.

Earlier this month, the head office of the central bank started doing re-discount business with the headquarters of major state banks, buying discount papers in the banks' hands to help increase liquidity in the markets.
The discount papers are commercial papers the banks buy from state-run enterprises.
"The expansion of the re-discount business is one of the important steps in China's financial reforms aimed at using indirect means to control money supply," said a central bank official.

The central bank has said it wants to expand the re-discount business by 50 percent in 1997 to allow the outstanding volume of re-discount papers to reach 60 billion yuan ($7.23 billion) by end-1997. The outstanding volume of re-discount papers was at 40 billion yuan the end of 1996.
Beijing plans to expand the Chinese yuan interbank market by admitting hundreds of city cooperative banks and branches of major state banks as members, a senior market official said.

The market, established in early 1996 to allow Chinese banks to move short-term funds among themselves, now has 20 state banks and 35 short-term financial centres, money brokerages run by the central bank, as members.
Daily volume on average is at around 2.5 billion yuan, far below a level that can make the market a barometer of China's short-term money supply, traders said.
The central bank also plans to expand its open market operations, started in April last year, by admitting 12 city cooperative banks into the system, local media have reported.
